subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Bacteria Lab
hook: Arjun observes bacteria doubling every hour in his school science lab. 2, 4, 8, 16... By day 10, the count is huge. Priya uses exponents to predict it: 2¹⁰ = 1024. How does she do it so fast?

slides.title: Doubling Bacteria Count
slides.storyContext: Arjun's biology class grows bacteria in a petri dish. Day 1: 2 cells. Day 2: 4. Day 3: 8. By day 5, he counts 32 cells. 'But how do I predict day 10 without counting all week?' Priya smiles: 'Use powers. On day 10, you'll have 2 to the power 10.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents are shortcuts for repeated multiplication.

slides.title: What is an Exponent?

points.label: Simple Meaning
points.text: An exponent tells you how many times to multiply a number by itself.

points.label: Parts of aⁿ
points.text: a = base (the number being multiplied). n = exponent (how many times).

points.label: Shortcut Power
points.text: Instead of writing 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, we write 2⁵. Much faster!

slides.inSimpleWords: aⁿ means 'a times itself n times.'

slides.title: Arjun's Lab Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun carefully records the bacteria count each day. 'Look at the pattern!' says Priya, pointing at his notebook. 'Day 1 is 2¹, day 2 is 2², day 3 is 2³. By day 10, it's 2¹⁰ = 1024 bacteria!' Arjun's eyes widen. 'That's incredible. Without exponents, I'd need a huge table.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Patterns in nature often follow exponential growth.

slides.title: Exponent Notation

points.label: Definition
points.text: aⁿ means 'a multiplied by itself n times.' a is the base, n is the exponent or power.

points.label: Reading
points.text: 2³ = 'two to the power three' or 'two cubed' = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8

points.label: Zero Exponent
points.text: Any number to the power 0 equals 1: a⁰ = 1 (e.g., 5⁰ = 1)

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents show how many times to multiply.

slides.title: Example 1: Bacteria Growth

example.problem: On day 6, Arjun has 2⁶ bacteria. Calculate the count.
example.solution: 2⁶ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64 bacteria on day 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 to the power 6 is 64 bacteria.

slides.title: Challenge 1: Find the Exponent

example.problem: On which day does Arjun have 128 bacteria? (Express as 2ⁿ where 128 = 2ⁿ)
example.solution: Count: 2 = 2¹, 4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 16 = 2⁴, 32 = 2⁵, 64 = 2⁶, 128 = 2⁷. So 128 bacteria appear on day 7.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find the exponent that gives you the target number.

slides.title: The Multiplication Rule
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun her magic trick. 'What if I want to calculate 2³ × 2²? Instead of computing each separately, there's a shortcut.' She writes: 2³ × 2² = (2×2×2) × (2×2) = 2⁵. 'The exponents add!' Arjun grins. 'So I just add 3 and 2 to get 5?'
slides.inSimpleWords: When multiplying powers with the same base, add exponents.

slides.title: Laws of Exponents

points.label: Multiplication Rule
points.text: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (multiply: add exponents). E.g., 2³ × 2² = 2⁵ = 32

points.label: Division Rule
points.text: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (divide: subtract exponents). E.g., 2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³ = 8

points.label: Power of Power
points.text: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐˣⁿ (raise to power: multiply exponents). E.g., (2²)³ = 2⁶ = 64

slides.inSimpleWords: Rules make big exponent problems simpler.

slides.title: Example 2: Applying Laws

example.problem: Simplify 3⁴ × 3². Then calculate the result.
example.solution: 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁴⁺² = 3⁶ = 729. Using the multiplication rule saves time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine exponents using the multiplication rule.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Division Rule

example.problem: Simplify 2⁷ ÷ 2³ using the division rule.
example.solution: 2⁷ ÷ 2³ = 2⁷⁻³ = 2⁴ = 16. The division rule lets you subtract exponents instead of dividing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use subtraction to divide powers of the same base.

slides.title: Power of Power
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Priya, 'What if I square a square? Like, if I have 2² and I square it again?' Priya thinks: '(2²)² means (2²) × (2²) = 4 × 4 = 16. But there's a faster way: multiply the exponents. 2² × ² = 2⁴ = 16.' Arjun nods. 'Every rule saves time!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Power of power means multiply the exponents.

slides.title: Example 3: Power of Power

example.problem: Evaluate (3²)³ using the power-of-power rule.
example.solution: (3²)³ = 3²ˣ³ = 3⁶ = 729. Multiply exponents 2 × 3 to get 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you raise a power to a power, multiply exponents.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Mixed Laws

example.problem: Simplify (2³)² × 2¹ and evaluate.
example.solution: (2³)² = 2⁶. Then 2⁶ × 2¹ = 2⁷ = 128. First apply power-of-power, then multiplication rule.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine multiple exponent rules in one problem.

slides.title: Special Exponents
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: 'What about exponent 0? What about negative exponents?' Priya flips through her notebook. 'Good questions. 2⁰ = 1 — any nonzero number to power 0 is 1. And 2⁻¹ = 1/2, a negative exponent flips the fraction.' Arjun writes this down carefully.
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponent 0 gives 1; negative exponents are fractions.

slides.title: Special Cases

points.label: Exponent 1
points.text: a¹ = a. E.g., 5¹ = 5, 12¹ = 12. The exponent 1 doesn't change the number.

points.label: Negative Exponent
points.text: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. E.g., 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. Negative flips to a fraction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Special exponents follow their own patterns.

slides.title: Example 4: Zero and Negative Exponents

example.problem: Evaluate 2⁰ and 2⁻² and 3⁰ × 2⁻¹.

slides.inSimpleWords: Special exponents have special values.

slides.title: Challenge 4: Apply All Rules

example.problem: Simplify (2³ × 2⁻¹) ÷ 2⁰.
example.solution: 2³ × 2⁻¹ = 2³⁺⁽⁻¹⁾ = 2² = 4. Then 2² ÷ 2⁰ = 2² ÷ 1 = 4. Any number ÷ 1 equals itself.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine multiplication, division, and special exponents.

slides.title: Big Numbers, Small Time
slides.storyContext: By the end of the week, Arjun's lab report is complete. The bacteria colony reaches 2¹⁰ = 1024 cells without needing a huge multiplication table. Priya says, 'That's the power of exponents. They let us express giant numbers compactly. Scientists use them for everything: atoms in a mole, stars in the universe, data storage capacity.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents let us write huge numbers simply.

slides.title: Real-World Use of Exponents

points.label: Science & Biology
points.text: Bacterial growth, viral spread, radioactive decay — all use exponential models.

points.label: Computer Science
points.text: Megabytes = 2²⁰ bytes, Gigabytes = 2³⁰ bytes. Storage capacity scales exponentially.

points.label: Finance
points.text: Compound interest uses exponents: A = P(1 + r)ᵗ. Money grows exponentially over time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents model real growth and scale.

slides.title: Example 5: Data Storage

example.problem: How many bytes are in 2 GB? (1 GB = 2³⁰ bytes)
example.solution: 2 GB = 2 × 2³⁰ bytes = 2¹ × 2³⁰ = 2³¹ bytes ≈ 2.1 billion bytes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Computer storage uses powers of 2.

slides.title: Challenge 5: Real Problem

example.problem: A virus infects 1 person, then 4 people, then 16, then 64. Express this as powers and find the pattern.
example.solution: Day 1: 4⁰ = 1. Day 2: 4¹ = 4. Day 3: 4² = 16. Day 4: 4³ = 64. Each day, the exponent increases by 1, and cases multiply by 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential spread happens faster than linear growth.

slides.title: Comparing Exponential and Linear Growth
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun a comparison graph. 'Look—if bacteria grew linearly (adding 2 each day), it'd be 2, 4, 6, 8, 10... after 10 days. But exponentially (multiplying by 2), it's 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024! Exponential beats linear by day 5.' Arjun realizes: 'This is why COVID spread so fast!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential growth accelerates much faster than linear.

slides.title: Exponential vs. Linear Growth

points.label: Linear Growth
points.text: Add the same amount each time: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Slow, steady, predictable.

points.label: Exponential Growth
points.text: Multiply by the same factor each time: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Accelerating, explosive.

points.label: Real Examples
points.text: Bacteria double (exponential). Saving money with interest (exponential). Decay of radioactive material (exponential).

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential growth accelerates rapidly.

slides.title: Challenge 6: Growth Comparison

example.problem: After 7 days, linear growth gives 14 (adding 2 each day). Exponential gives 2⁷ = 128. Which grows faster by day 10?
example.solution: Linear at day 10: 20 (adding 2 each day). Exponential: 2¹⁰ = 1024. Exponential is 51 times larger! Exponential always dominates in the long run.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential growth beats linear growth every time.

slides.title: Power Play Summary

points.text: Exponents aⁿ replace repeated multiplication.
Laws of exponents simplify big calculations.
Arjun predicts bacteria; Priya predicts using powers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents make patterns and growth easy.

subject: Mathematics
title: Building Mumbai's Community Center
hook: Arjun's uncle is renovating a community center in Mumbai. He needs to choose between square, rectangular, and diamond-shaped plots. Priya explains the angle and side properties. Which shape is sturdiest?

slides.title: Choosing the Plot Shape
slides.storyContext: Arjun's uncle shows three land plots for the community center: one perfectly square, one rectangular, and one diamond-shaped (rhombus). 'Which is strongest?' he asks. Priya pulls out her geometry notes: 'It depends on their angles and sides. All quadrilaterals have 4 sides and angles summing to 360°.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Quadrilaterals are 4-sided closed figures.

slides.title: What is a Quadrilateral?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A quadrilateral is a polygon with exactly 4 sides and 4 angles.

points.label: Closed Figure
points.text: All sides connect to form a closed loop. No gaps, no intersections.

points.label: Common Examples
points.text: Squares, rectangles, rhombuses, trapezoids, parallelograms — all are quadrilaterals.

slides.inSimpleWords: A quadrilateral has 4 sides and 4 angles.

slides.title: Arjun's Angle Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun measures the angles on his uncle's three plots using Priya's protractor. Square: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°. Rectangle: same! Diamond: 60° + 120° + 60° + 120° = 360°. 'Wait, they all add to 360°!' Arjun exclaims. Priya nods: 'That's the angle sum property of all quadrilaterals.'
slides.inSimpleWords: All quadrilateral angles sum to 360°.

slides.title: Angle Sum Property

points.label: Rule
points.text: Sum of all interior angles in any quadrilateral = 360°

points.label: Proof Context
points.text: Divide any quadrilateral into 2 triangles. Each triangle = 180°. Total = 360°.

points.label: Example
points.text: Rectangle: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°. Diamond (rhombus): all 4 angles also sum to 360°.

slides.inSimpleWords: All 4 angles in a quadrilateral add to 360°.

slides.title: Example 1: Finding Unknown Angle

example.problem: A quadrilateral has angles 80°, 100°, and 75°. Find the 4th angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find missing angles using the 360° rule.

slides.title: Challenge 1: Angle Hunt

example.problem: A quadrilateral has three equal angles of 90° each. What is the 4th angle?
example.solution: 360° - (90° + 90° + 90°) = 360° - 270° = 90°. All four angles are 90°, so it's a rectangle or square.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the 360° rule to find any missing angle.

slides.title: Four Types of Quadrilaterals
slides.storyContext: Arjun's uncle decides to study each shape carefully. Priya draws four diagrams: a perfect square, a stretched rectangle, a tilted diamond, and a slanted four-sider. 'Look at their sides and angles. They're all different.' She explains how squares are special (all equal sides, all right angles), rectangles are flexible (opposite sides equal), and rhombuses and trapezoids have their own rules.
slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals have different properties.

slides.title: Types of Quadrilaterals

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles (90° each). Most stable for building.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: Opposite sides equal, 4 right angles. Flexible length-to-width ratio.

points.label: Rhombus (Diamond)
points.text: 4 equal sides but angles NOT all 90°. Angles come in pairs (opposite angles equal).

points.label: Trapezium
points.text: One pair of parallel sides. Most irregular of the common types.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals have different properties.

slides.title: Example 2: Rhombus Angles

example.problem: A rhombus plot has two angles of 60° each. Find the other two angles.
example.solution: In a rhombus, opposite angles are equal. If 2 angles = 60°, then 60° + 60° + ? + ? = 360°. The other two angles = (360° - 120°) ÷ 2 = 120° each.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhombus has opposite angles that are equal.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Rectangle or Square?

example.problem: A plot has all 90° angles and all equal sides. What type of quadrilateral is it?
example.solution: A square. It has all right angles (rectangle property) AND all equal sides (rhombus property). When both are true, it's a square.

slides.inSimpleWords: A square combines rectangle and rhombus properties.

slides.title: Opposite Sides and Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya explains a key property: 'In a parallelogram—and rhombuses are special parallelograms—opposite sides are parallel and opposite angles are equal.' Arjun draws this: 'So if one angle is 70°, its opposite is also 70°?' 'Exactly,' Priya confirms. 'And the other two angles are both 110°, since 70° + 110° = 180°.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite sides and angles have matching properties.

slides.title: Parallelogram Properties

points.label: Opposite Sides Equal
points.text: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal in length and parallel.

points.label: Opposite Angles Equal
points.text: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal. Angles on the same side sum to 180°.

points.label: Diagonals
points.text: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other (cross at midpoints).

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallelograms have matching opposite sides and angles.

slides.title: Example 3: Parallelogram Angles

example.problem: A parallelogram plot has one angle of 75°. Find all four angles.
example.solution: Opposite angle = 75° (opposite angles equal). Adjacent angles = 180° - 75° = 105° each. So angles are: 75°, 105°, 75°, 105°.

slides.inSimpleWords: One angle determines all others in a parallelogram.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Diagonal Bisection

example.problem: In a parallelogram, one diagonal is divided into segments of 5 cm and 5 cm at the crossing point. What is the other diagonal's length at its crossing point?
example.solution: Since diagonals bisect each other, each half of the crossing diagonal is 5 cm. The full length is 10 cm. (Each half is equal length.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Diagonals split equally at their intersection.

slides.title: Trapezium: The Unique One
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks about the trapezium shape. Priya explains: 'A trapezium has only ONE pair of parallel sides, unlike a parallelogram which has TWO pairs. This makes it less stable for building, but useful for other designs.' She shows him examples from Indian architecture where trapezium shapes appear.
slides.inSimpleWords: Trapeziums have only one pair of parallel sides.

slides.title: Trapezium and Other Quadrilaterals

points.label: Trapezium
points.text: Exactly one pair of parallel sides. Angles don't have simple relationships like parallelograms.

points.label: Kite
points.text: Two pairs of adjacent equal sides. Diagonals perpendicular. Only one pair of opposite angles equal.

points.label: Irregular Quadrilateral
points.text: No parallel sides, no equal sides. Only guaranteed property: angles sum to 360°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Other quadrilaterals have unique properties.

slides.title: Example 4: Trapezium Angles

example.problem: A trapezium has angles 50°, 130°, 70°. Find the 4th angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Any quadrilateral angles sum to 360°.

slides.title: Challenge 4: Real Building Decision

example.problem: Arjun's uncle must choose: square (all sides 10m, all angles 90°) or rectangle (10m × 15m, all angles 90°). Which encloses more area for the community center?
example.solution: Square area = 10 × 10 = 100 m². Rectangle area = 10 × 15 = 150 m². Rectangle encloses more but uses more materials. Depends on the budget.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different shapes enclose different areas.

slides.title: The Perfect Choice
slides.storyContext: After studying all types, Arjun's uncle decides: 'The main building is square (strongest, equal sides), but the courtyard will be rectangular (flexible, fits the street boundary). The rhombus will be decorative (beautiful angles).' Priya smiles. 'Each shape serves its purpose. Understanding their properties helps you choose wisely.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals suit different purposes.

slides.title: Perimeter and Area Basics

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all four sides. Square with side 10m: 10+10+10+10 = 40m. Rectangle 10×15: 10+15+10+15 = 50m.

points.label: Area of Square
points.text: side². Square with side 10m: 10² = 100 m².

points.label: Area of Rectangle
points.text: length × width. Rectangle 10m × 15m: 10 × 15 = 150 m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is around; area is inside.

slides.title: Example 5: Building Plot Comparison

example.problem: A square plot costs Rs 500/m² and a rectangular plot costs Rs 400/m². Square is 20m on each side; rectangle is 20m × 30m. Which is more expensive?
example.solution: Square area: 20² = 400 m². Cost: 400 × 500 = Rs 2,00,000. Rectangle area: 20 × 30 = 600 m². Cost: 600 × 400 = Rs 2,40,000. Rectangle is more expensive but larger.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare area and cost for practical decisions.

slides.title: Challenge 5: Complete Plot Design

example.problem: A plot must be rectangular, 20m long. If the builder wants 300 m² area, what should the width be? What's the perimeter?
example.solution: Area = length × width. 300 = 20 × width. Width = 15m. Perimeter = 20+15+20+15 = 70m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use formulas to find missing dimensions.

slides.title: Symmetry in Quadrilaterals
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices something beautiful. 'The square looks the same from every angle. But the rectangle only looks the same if you flip it sideways.' Priya nods: 'That's symmetry. Squares have 4-fold rotational symmetry; rectangles have 2-fold. Rhombuses also have 2-fold. Symmetry makes shapes beautiful AND strong.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry is a hidden property of shapes.

slides.title: Symmetry in Quadrilaterals

points.label: Line Symmetry
points.text: Mirror reflection through a line. Square has 4 lines of symmetry. Rectangle has 2. Rhombus has 2.

points.label: Rotational Symmetry
points.text: Shape looks same after rotation. Square: 90° rotation. Rectangle: 180°. Trapezium: usually none.

points.label: Architectural Use
points.text: Symmetrical designs are aesthetically pleasing and structurally balanced.

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry reveals hidden geometry.

slides.title: Quadrilaterals Overview

points.text: All quadrilaterals have 4 sides and angles summing to 360°.
Squares and rectangles are most stable for construction.
Each type has unique angle and side properties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quadrilaterals are essential shapes in building.

subject: Mathematics
title: The School Lunch Mystery
hook: The school lunch manager in Delhi needs to divide 144 chapatis equally among students. Priya and Arjun discover divisibility shortcuts: 144 is even (divisible by 2), sums digits to 9 (divisible by 9). How many ways can they divide the chapatis?

slides.title: Dividing Lunch Equally
slides.storyContext: The school has 144 chapatis to serve for lunch. The manager asks: 'Can I divide them equally among 8 students? Among 9? Among 5?' Priya flips through her number tricks notebook: 'Let me check the divisibility rules. 144 ends in 4, so it's even (divisible by 2). Add digits: 1+4+4=9, divisible by 9!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules find factors without dividing.

slides.title: What is Divisibility?

points.label: Simple Definition
points.text: A number is divisible by another if it divides evenly with no remainder. 8 is divisible by 2 (8÷2=4, no remainder).

points.label: Factor
points.text: If a divides b evenly, then a is a factor (or divisor) of b. Factors help us find all ways to divide a number.

points.label: Why It Matters
points.text: Finding factors quickly lets us solve word problems (like dividing chapatis) without actual division.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility tells if one number divides another evenly.

slides.title: The Shortcut Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks, 'Do I need to actually divide 144 by every number to check? That's slow.' Priya shows him her notebook: 'Rules! Every digit divisible by 2 ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Every number whose digits sum to 3 (or 9) is divisible by 3 (or 9). Shortcuts save time.' Arjun's eyes widen. 'This is like cheating, but math-allowed!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules are quick shortcuts.

slides.title: Divisibility Rules

points.label: Divisibility by 2
points.text: Number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. E.g., 144 ends in 4 → divisible by 2.

points.label: Divisibility by 3
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 3. E.g., 144: 1+4+4=9 (divisible by 3) → 144 divisible by 3.

points.label: Divisibility by 9
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 9. E.g., 144: 1+4+4=9 → divisible by 9.

points.label: Divisibility by 5
points.text: Number ends in 0 or 5. E.g., 145 ends in 5 → divisible by 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quick tricks test if numbers divide evenly.

slides.title: Example 1: Chapati Division

example.problem: Check if 144 chapatis can be divided equally among 9 students.
example.solution: Use divisibility by 9: sum of digits = 1+4+4 = 9. Since 9 is divisible by 9, 144 is divisible by 9. Each student gets 144÷9 = 16 chapatis.

slides.inSimpleWords: 144 divided by 9 gives exactly 16 per student.

slides.title: Challenge 1: Divisibility Check

example.problem: Is 240 divisible by 5? Is it divisible by 3? By 9?
example.solution: By 5: ends in 0 → YES. By 3: 2+4+0=6 (divisible by 3) → YES. By 9: 6 is not divisible by 9 → NO.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply each rule to find divisibility quickly.

slides.title: Prime vs Composite
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: 'Can I break down every number into smaller factors? Or are some numbers special?' Priya explains: 'Some numbers have only 2 factors: 1 and themselves. We call them primes. Others have many factors. Those are composite. It's like some numbers are building blocks; others are made FROM blocks.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers are either prime or composite.

slides.title: Prime vs. Composite

points.label: Prime Number
points.text: A number with exactly 2 factors: 1 and itself. E.g., 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 are prime.

points.label: Composite Number
points.text: A number with more than 2 factors. E.g., 4 (factors: 1,2,4), 6 (factors: 1,2,3,6), 144 (many factors).

points.label: 1 is Special
points.text: 1 has only 1 factor (itself), so it's neither prime nor composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes have 2 factors; composites have more.

slides.title: Example 2: Prime Check

example.problem: Is 17 a prime number? List all its factors.
example.solution: Factors of 17: 1 and 17 only. Since it has exactly 2 factors, 17 is prime. (No other number divides 17 evenly.)

slides.inSimpleWords: 17 is prime because only 1 and 17 divide it.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Identify the Type

example.problem: Is 20 prime or composite? List all its factors.
example.solution: Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. That's 6 factors (more than 2), so 20 is composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count factors to decide prime vs. composite.

slides.title: Finding All Factors
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: 'To divide 144 chapatis fairly, I need ALL ways to split them. That means finding every factor. 144 = 1×144, 2×72, 3×48, 4×36, 6×24, 8×18, 9×16, 12×12. Each pair tells us how to divide.' Arjun realizes: 'So there are 15 different ways to divide them!'
slides.inSimpleWords: All factor pairs show ways to divide a number.

slides.title: Finding All Factors

points.label: Factor Pairs
points.text: If a × b = n, then a and b are a factor pair of n. For 144: 1×144, 2×72, 3×48, etc.

points.label: Systematic Method
points.text: Start with 1 and n. Then check 2, 3, 4... up to √n. When you find a factor, its pair automatically exists.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Factor pairs help in division problems, simplifying fractions, finding GCD and LCM.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every factor has a pair that multiplies to the number.

slides.title: Example 3: Factor Pairs

example.problem: Find all factors of 24.
example.solution: Pairs: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6. So all factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 (8 factors total).

slides.inSimpleWords: List all factor pairs to find all factors.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Factor Hunt

example.problem: How many ways can 36 chapatis be divided among students (equal per student)? List all possibilities.
example.solution: Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Each represents a group size: 36 groups of 1, 18 groups of 2, 12 groups of 3, 9 groups of 4, 6 groups of 6, 4 groups of 9, 3 groups of 12, 2 groups of 18, 1 group of 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each factor shows one way to divide.

slides.title: GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: The manager asks a tricky question: 'If I have 144 chapatis and 120 cookies, how can I divide them into equal boxes with no leftovers?' Priya explains: 'Find the GCD—Greatest Common Divisor. 144 and 120 both divide by 24. So we make 6 boxes with 24 chapatis and 5 cookies each.' Arjun nods: 'One tool, multiple problems!'
slides.inSimpleWords: GCD helps divide multiple quantities fairly.

slides.title: GCD and LCM Basics

points.label: GCD (Greatest Common Divisor)
points.text: Largest number that divides both numbers evenly. GCD(144, 120) = 24. Useful for fair division.

points.label: LCM (Least Common Multiple)
points.text: Smallest number divisible by both. LCM(12, 18) = 36. Useful for syncing cycles.

points.label: Finding GCD
points.text: List factors of both numbers; pick the largest common one. Or use Euclidean algorithm for bigger numbers.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD and LCM solve real-world grouping problems.

slides.title: Example 4: GCD Application

example.problem: Find GCD(36, 48). Use it to arrange items into equal boxes.
example.solution: Factors of 36: 1,2,3,4,6,9,12,18,36. Factors of 48: 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,48. GCD = 12. So make 12 boxes: 3 items of type A, 4 items of type B per box.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the largest common factor.

slides.title: Challenge 4: GCD Problem

example.problem: A bakery has 60 cookies and 80 cupcakes. What's the largest number of identical boxes they can fill with no remainder?

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD finds the largest equal-group size.

slides.title: Prime Factorization

slides.title: Prime Factorization

points.label: Definition
points.text: Expressing a number as a product of prime numbers. E.g., 144 = 2⁴ × 3² = 16 × 9.

points.label: Prime Factorization Process
points.text: Divide by smallest primes (2, 3, 5, 7...) repeatedly until you reach 1. All composite numbers have unique factorization.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Finding GCD, LCM, simplifying fractions, understanding number structure.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break numbers into their prime building blocks.

slides.title: Challenge 5: Factorization Chain

example.problem: Prime factorize 72 and 48. Use them to find GCD(72,48).
example.solution: 72 = 2³ × 3². 48 = 2⁴ × 3. Common factors: 2³ × 3 = 8 × 3 = 24. So GCD = 24.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime factors help find GCD easily.

slides.title: Real-World Number Secrets
slides.storyContext: Priya concludes: 'Numbers hide patterns everywhere. Primes protect your passwords (RSA encryption uses large primes). Divisibility rules save time in accounting. GCD/LCM solve real problems: scheduling buses, dividing resources. Math isn't abstract—it's practical magic.' Arjun smiles. 'The lunch mystery revealed the power of numbers!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Number properties solve real-world problems.

slides.title: Challenge 6: Complete Number Detective

example.problem: A number is divisible by both 6 and 8. Is it divisible by 24? What's the LCM(6,8)?
example.solution: If divisible by both 6 and 8, it's divisible by LCM(6,8). 6=2×3, 8=2³. LCM=2³×3=24. Yes, it's divisible by 24. LCM tells the smallest common multiple.

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM finds the smallest common multiple.
